paragraphs: About fifteen years ago, late in August or early in September, a train stopped at Wilsthorpe, a country station in eastern England. Among the passengers who got out was a rather tall, reasonably good-looking young man carrying a small bag and some papers tied into a packet. From the way he looked about him, one would have said he expected someone to meet him. Just as plainly, he was expected. The stationmaster ran forward a step or two, then seemed to remember himself. He turned and beckoned to a stout, self-important man with a short, round beard, who was looking along the train in some bewilderment. “Mr Cooper,” he called, “Mr Cooper, I think this is your gentleman.” Then, to the passenger who had just stepped down, “Mr Humphreys, sir? Glad to welcome you to Wilsthorpe. There’s a cart from the Hall for your luggage, and here’s Mr Cooper, who I think you know.” Mr Cooper had hurried over. He now raised his hat and shook hands. “Very pleased, I’m sure,” he said, “to echo Mr Palmer’s kind words. I should have been the first to give them expression, but your face was not familiar to me, Mr Humphreys. May your residence among us be marked as a red-letter day, sir.” “Thank you very much, Mr Cooper,” Humphreys said, “for your good wishes, and Mr Palmer too. I do very much hope that this change of—er—tenancy—which you must all regret, I’m sure—will not be to the disadvantage of those with whom I shall come into contact.” He stopped, feeling that his words were not fitting together very happily. Mr Cooper broke in. “Oh, you may rest assured of that, Mr Humphreys. I’ll take it upon myself to assure you, sir, that a warm welcome awaits you on every side. And as for any change of propriety proving harmful to the neighbourhood, well, your late uncle—” Here Mr Cooper also stopped, perhaps in obedience to an inner warning, perhaps because Mr Palmer cleared his throat loudly and asked Humphreys for his ticket. The two men left the little station and, at Humphreys’s suggestion, decided to walk to Mr Cooper’s house, where lunch was waiting.

The relationship between these people can be explained in a few lines. Quite unexpectedly, Humphreys had inherited an estate from an uncle. He had never seen either the estate or the uncle. He was alone in the world, a capable, kindly man whose work in a government office over the last four or five years had done little to prepare him for life as a country gentleman. He was studious, rather shy, and had few outdoor interests apart from golf and gardening. Today he had come to Wilsthorpe for the first time to discuss matters needing immediate attention with Mr Cooper, the estate manager. Why, one might ask, was this his first visit? Should he not, out of common decency, have attended his uncle’s funeral? The answer is simple. He had been abroad when his uncle died, and his address could not immediately be found. So he had put off coming to Wilsthorpe until he heard that everything was ready for him. And now we find him at Mr Cooper’s comfortable house, opposite the rectory, having just shaken hands with the smiling Mrs and Miss Cooper.
During the few minutes before lunch was announced, they settled into elaborate chairs in the sitting room. Humphreys, aware that he was being assessed, quietly perspired.
“I was just saying to Mr Humphreys, my dear,” Mr Cooper said, “that I hope and trust his residence among us here in Wilsthorpe will be marked as a red-letter day.”
“Yes, indeed, I’m sure,” Mrs Cooper said warmly, “and many, many of them.”

Miss Cooper murmured something similar. Humphreys tried a joke about painting the whole calendar red. Although it was greeted with shrill laughter, it had clearly not been fully understood. At this point they went in to lunch.
“Do you know this part of the country at all, Mr Humphreys?” Mrs Cooper asked after a short interval. This was a better opening.
“No, I’m sorry to say I don’t,” Humphreys replied. “What I could see from the train seemed very pleasant.”

“Oh, it is a pleasant part. Really, I sometimes say I don’t know a nicer district, as countryside goes. And the people around here, too—there’s always so much going on. But I’m afraid you’ve come a little late for some of the better garden parties, Mr Humphreys.”

“I suppose I have. Dear me, what a pity!” Humphreys said with a gleam of relief. Then, feeling that he could get a little more out of this subject, he added, “But after all, you see, Mrs Cooper, even if I could have come earlier, I should have had to keep away from them, shouldn’t I? My poor uncle’s recent death, you know—”

“Oh dear, Mr Humphreys, of course! What a dreadful thing for me to say!” Mr and Miss Cooper made inarticulate sounds of agreement. “What must you have thought? I’m so sorry. You really must forgive me.”

“Not at all, Mrs Cooper, I assure you. I can’t honestly say that my uncle’s death was a great grief to me, because I had never seen him. I only meant that I supposed I shouldn’t be expected to take part in festivities of that kind for a little while.”
“Now, really, it’s very kind of you to take it that way, Mr Humphreys, isn’t it, George? And you do forgive me? But just imagine! You never saw poor old Mr Wilson!”

“Never in my life. I never even had a letter from him. But, by the way, you have something to forgive me for. I’ve never thanked you, except by letter, for all the trouble you’ve taken to find people to look after me at the Hall.”

“Oh, I’m sure that was nothing, Mr Humphreys. But I really think you’ll find them satisfactory. We’ve known the man and his wife for a number of years, and have engaged them as your butler and housekeeper. Such a nice, respectable couple. And Mr Cooper can certainly vouch for the men in the stables and gardens.”

“Yes, Mr Humphreys, they’re a good lot. The head gardener is the only one who’s stayed on from Mr Wilson’s time. As you no doubt saw in the will, most of the employees received legacies from the old gentleman and retired from their posts. And, as my wife says, your housekeeper and butler are likely to give you every satisfaction.”

“So everything is ready for you to move in this very day, Mr Humphreys, as I understood you wished,” Mrs Cooper said. “Everything except company, that is. I’m afraid you’ll find yourself quite at a loss there. Only, we understood that you intended to move in at once. Otherwise, I’m sure you know we should have been only too pleased to have you stay here.”

“I’m quite sure you would, Mrs Cooper, and I’m very grateful. But I thought I really had better take the plunge at once. I’m used to living alone, and there will be quite enough to occupy my evenings for some time—looking through papers and books and so on. I thought, if Mr Cooper could spare the time this afternoon to go over the house and grounds with me—”
“Certainly, certainly, Mr Humphreys. My time is yours, until any hour you please.”
“Until dinner time, Father, you mean,” Miss Cooper said. “Don’t forget we’re going to the Brasnetts’. And have you got all the garden keys?”
“Are you a skilled gardener, Miss Cooper?” Mr Humphreys asked. “I wish you would tell me what to expect at the Hall.”

“Oh, I don’t know about a skilled gardener, Mr Humphreys. I’m very fond of flowers. But I often say the Hall garden could be made quite lovely. It’s very old-fashioned as it is, with a great deal of shrubbery. There’s an old temple too, and a maze.”
“Really? Have you ever explored it?”

“No-o,” Miss Cooper said, drawing in her lips and shaking her head. “I’ve often longed to try, but old Mr Wilson always kept it locked. He wouldn’t even let Lady Wardrop in. She lives nearby, at Bentley, you know, and she’s a really skilled gardener, if you like. That’s why I asked Father whether he had all the keys.”
“I see. Well, I clearly must look into that, and show you round when I’ve learnt the way.”

“Oh, thank you so much, Mr Humphreys! Now I shall have the laugh on Miss Foster—that’s our rector’s daughter, you know. They’re away on holiday now. Such nice people. We always had a joke between us about which of us would be first to get into the maze.”

“I think the garden keys must be up at the house,” Mr Cooper said, having examined a large bunch. “There are a number in the library. Now, Mr Humphreys, if you’re ready, we might say goodbye to these ladies and set out on our little tour of exploration.”

As they came out of Mr Cooper’s front gate, Humphreys had to run the gauntlet of the villagers. There was no organised demonstration, but plenty of hats were touched and many careful looks cast by the men and women gathered in unusually large numbers along the street. He also had to exchange a few words with the lodge-keeper’s wife as they passed the park gates, and with the lodge-keeper himself, who was tending the park road. I cannot, however, spare the time to report their progress in full. During the half-mile or so between the lodge and the house, Humphreys found an opportunity to ask a question that brought up his late uncle. Before long, Mr Cooper had launched into a lengthy explanation.

“It’s strange to think, as my wife was saying just now, that you should never have seen the old gentleman. And yet—I’m confident you won’t misunderstand me, Mr Humphreys—I don’t think you and he would have had very much in common. Not that I have a word to say against him—not a single word. I can tell you what he was,” Mr Cooper said, stopping suddenly and fixing his eyes on Humphreys. “I can tell you what he was in a nutshell, as the saying goes. He was a complete, thorough health worrier. That describes him to a T. That’s what he was, sir, a complete health worrier. No participation in what went on around him. I did venture, I believe, to send you a little cutting from our local paper, which I took the opportunity of contributing when he died. If I remember rightly, that was very much the substance of it. But don’t, Mr Humphreys,” Cooper continued, tapping him impressively on the chest, “don’t run away with the impression that I wish to say anything but what is most creditable—most creditable—to your respected uncle and my late employer. Upright, Mr Humphreys—open as the day. Generous to everyone in his dealings. He had the heart to feel and the hand to help. But there it was. There was the stumbling block—his unfortunate health, or, as I might more truly put it, his lack of health.”
“Yes, poor man. Did he suffer from any particular disorder before his last illness? That, I take it, was little more than old age?”

“Exactly that, Mr Humphreys, exactly that. The flash slowly flickering away in the pan,” Cooper said, with what he considered a suitable gesture, “the golden bowl gradually ceasing to vibrate. But I should answer your other question in the negative. A general lack of vitality? Yes. A particular complaint? No, unless you count a nasty cough he had. Why, we’re practically at the house. A handsome mansion, wouldn’t you say, Mr Humphreys?”

On the whole, it deserved the description, though its proportions were odd. It was a very tall red-brick house, with a plain parapet almost entirely concealing the roof. It looked like a town house set down in the country. There was a basement and a rather imposing flight of steps to the front door. Its height also made it look as though it needed wings on either side, but there were none. Trees hid the stables and other outbuildings. Humphreys guessed that it dated from about 1770.

The mature couple engaged as butler and cook-housekeeper were waiting inside the front door. They opened it as their new employer approached. Humphreys already knew that their name was Calton, and their appearance and manner impressed him favourably during their brief conversation. They agreed that next day he should go through the silverware and the wine cellar with Mr Calton, while Mrs C. should talk to him about linen, bedding and so on—what they had and what they needed. Then, dismissing the Caltons for the moment, he and Cooper began to look through the house. Its layout is not important to this story. The large ground-floor rooms were satisfactory, particularly the library. It was as big as the dining room and had three tall windows facing east. The bedroom prepared for Humphreys was directly above it. There were many pleasant old pictures and a few genuinely interesting ones. None of the furniture was new, and hardly any of the books dated from later than the seventies. After seeing and hearing about the few changes his uncle had made, and studying a shiny portrait of him in the sitting room, Humphreys had to agree with Cooper. In all probability, he would have found little to attract him in his predecessor. It made him rather sad that he could not be sorry—he grieved at being unable to grieve—for the man who had contributed so much to his well-being, whether or not he had felt kindly towards his unknown nephew. For Humphreys felt that he could be happy at Wilsthorpe, perhaps especially happy in its library.

Now it was time to inspect the garden. The empty stables and the laundry could wait. So they turned their attention to the garden, and it soon became clear that Miss Cooper had been right about its possibilities. Mr Cooper had also done well to keep the gardener on. The late Mr Wilson might not have shared the newest ideas about gardening—plainly he had not—but everything here had been done under a knowledgeable eye. The equipment and the stock of plants were excellent. Cooper was delighted by Humphreys’s evident pleasure and the suggestions he occasionally made. “I can see you’ve found your calling here, Mr Humphreys,” he said. “You’ll make this place a regular showpiece before many more seasons have passed over our heads. I wish Clutterham had been here—that’s the head gardener. Of course, as I told you, he would have been, if his son hadn’t been out of commission with a fever, poor fellow! I should have liked him to hear what you think of the place.”

“Yes, you told me he couldn’t be here today, and I was very sorry to hear why. But tomorrow will be time enough. What’s that white building on the mound at the end of the grassy avenue? Is it the temple Miss Cooper mentioned?”

“That it is, Mr Humphreys—the Temple of Friendship. Your late uncle’s grandfather built it from marble brought from Italy for the purpose. Would you perhaps care to walk over? It gives a very sweet view of the park.”

The temple’s general design resembled the Temple of the Sibyl at Tivoli, with a dome added, though the whole building was considerably smaller. Some ancient tomb carvings had been built into its wall, and it all had a pleasant flavour of the grand tour. Cooper produced the key and opened the heavy door with some difficulty. Inside was a handsome ceiling, but little furniture. Most of the floor was taken up by a pile of thick, round stone blocks. Each had a single letter cut deeply into its slightly rounded upper surface. “What do these mean?” Humphreys asked.

“Mean? Well, we’re told that everything has its purpose, Mr Humphreys, and I suppose these blocks have had theirs like anything else. But as for what that purpose is or was”—here Mr Cooper took on the manner of a lecturer—“I, for one, should be at a loss to tell you, sir. All I know about them can be summed up in very few words. It is simply this: they are said to have been removed from the maze by your late uncle, before I came on the scene. That, Mr Humphreys, is—”
“Oh, the maze!” Humphreys exclaimed. “I’d forgotten that. We must have a look at it. Where is it?”
Cooper drew him to the temple door and pointed with his stick. “Guide your eye,” he said, rather in the manner of the Second Elder in Handel’s Susanna—
Far to the west direct your straining eyes, where that tall holm oak rises to the skies.

“Guide your eye along my stick here, and follow the line straight opposite where we’re standing. I guarantee, Mr Humphreys, that you’ll catch sight of the arch over the entrance. It’s just at the end of the walk corresponding to the one that leads to this very building. Were you thinking of going there at once? If so, I must go to the house and fetch the key. If you walk on there, I’ll join you in a few moments.”

Humphreys accordingly strolled down the avenue leading from the temple, past the garden side of the house and up the grassy approach to the arch Cooper had pointed out. He was surprised to find a high wall around the entire maze, and a padlocked iron gate in the archway. Then he remembered Miss Cooper’s account of his uncle’s refusal to let anyone into this part of the garden. He reached the gate, but Cooper had still not arrived. For a few minutes he occupied himself by reading the motto cut over the entrance—“My secret is for me and the sons of my house”—and trying to remember its source. Then he grew impatient and considered climbing the wall. That was clearly not worth doing. It might have been possible if he had been wearing an older suit. Or could he force the padlock, which was very old? Apparently not. Yet when he gave the gate one last irritated kick, something gave way and the lock fell at his feet. He pushed the gate open, inconveniencing a number of nettles as he did so, and stepped inside the enclosure.

It was a circular maze of yew, with hedges that had long gone untrimmed and had grown outwards and upwards to a most unconventional width and height. The paths, too, were almost impassable. Humphreys could force his way along them only by completely ignoring scratches, nettle stings and wet. Still, he reflected, this would at least make it easier to find his way out, because he was leaving a very obvious trail. As far as he could remember, he had never been in a maze before. Nor did he now feel that he had missed much. The damp, darkness and smell of crushed goosegrass and nettles were anything but cheerful. Still, this did not seem a particularly complicated example of its kind. Here he was—was that Cooper arriving at last, by the way? No!—almost at its heart, without having thought much about which path he was taking. Ah, there at last was the centre, easily reached. And there was something to reward him. At first he thought the central ornament was a sundial. But when he brushed away some of the thick growth of brambles and bindweed covering it, he saw that it was something less ordinary. A stone column stood about four feet high, with a metal globe on top—copper, judging by its green coating. It was engraved, and finely engraved too, with outlined figures and lettering. That was what Humphreys saw. A brief look at the figures convinced him that it was one of those mysterious objects called celestial globes, from which, one would suppose, nobody had ever learnt anything about the heavens. But it was too dark, at least in the maze, to examine this curiosity closely. Besides, he could now hear Cooper’s voice, accompanied by noises like an elephant in the jungle. Humphreys called to him to follow the trail he had made. Soon Cooper appeared, panting, in the central circle. He apologised profusely for the delay. After all, he had been unable to find the key. “But there!” he said. “You’ve penetrated to the heart of the mystery unaided and unanointed, as the saying goes. Well! I suppose it must be thirty or forty years since a human foot trod these grounds. Certainly I’ve never set foot in them before. Well, well! What’s that old proverb about angels fearing to tread? It’s been proved true once again.” Short as Humphreys’s acquaintance with Cooper was, it was enough to assure him that the allusion contained no malice. He refrained from making the obvious remark. Instead, he suggested that it was high time to return to the house for a late cup of tea and release Cooper for his evening engagement. They left the maze, finding it almost as easy to retrace their path as it had been to come in.
“Have you any idea,” Humphreys asked as they walked towards the house, “why my uncle kept that place so carefully locked?”
Cooper stopped, and Humphreys felt that a revelation must be coming.

“I should only be deceiving you, Mr Humphreys, and to no good purpose, if I claimed to possess any information whatsoever on that subject. When I first took up my duties here, some eighteen years ago, the maze was word for word in the condition you see now. The only time the question ever came up, to my knowledge, was the occasion my daughter mentioned to you. Lady Wardrop—I haven’t a word to say against her—wrote asking to enter the maze. Your uncle showed me the note. A most polite note, everything one could expect from such a quarter. ‘Cooper,’ he said, ‘I wish you would answer this note for me.’ ‘Certainly, Mr Wilson,’ I said, for I was quite used to acting as his secretary. ‘What answer shall I give?’ ‘Well,’ he said, ‘give Lady Wardrop my compliments. Tell her that if that part of the grounds is ever put in order, I shall be happy to give her the first opportunity to see it. But it has been closed for a number of years, and I shall be grateful if she will kindly not press the matter.’ That, Mr Humphreys, was your good uncle’s last word on the subject. I don’t think I can add anything.” After a pause, Cooper went on, “Unless it is just this: as far as I could judge, he disliked the memory of his grandfather, as people often will, for one reason or another. As I mentioned, it was his grandfather who had the maze laid out. A man of peculiar beliefs, Mr Humphreys, and a great traveller. This coming Sunday you’ll have the opportunity to see his memorial tablet in our little parish church. It was put up a long time after his death.”
“Oh! I should have expected someone so fond of building to have designed a mausoleum for himself.”

“Well, I’ve never noticed anything of that kind. In fact, now I think of it, I’m not at all sure his resting place is anywhere within our boundaries. I’m pretty certain he doesn’t lie in the vault. Strange, now, that I shouldn’t be able to give you information on that point! Still, after all, we can’t say it’s a matter of crucial importance where the poor mortal coils are laid, can we, Mr Humphreys?”
At this point they entered the house, interrupting Cooper’s speculations.

Tea was ready in the library, where Mr Cooper turned to subjects suited to the surroundings. “A fine collection of books! One of the finest in this part of the country, I understand from experts. Splendid illustrations in some of them, too. I remember your uncle showing me a book of views of foreign towns. Most absorbing, and produced in first-rate style. And another, all done by hand, with the ink as fresh as if it had been put on yesterday. Yet he told me it was the work of an old monk, hundreds of years ago. I’ve always taken a keen interest in literature myself. To my mind, there’s hardly anything to compare with a good hour’s reading after a hard day’s work. Far better than wasting the whole evening at a friend’s house—which reminds me! I shall be in trouble with my wife if I don’t hurry home and get ready to squander one of those very evenings! I must be off, Mr Humphreys.”
“And that reminds me,” Humphreys said, “if I’m to show Miss Cooper the maze tomorrow, we must have it cleared a little. Could you mention that to whoever should attend to it?”

“Why, certainly. A couple of men with scythes could clear a path tomorrow morning. I’ll leave word as I pass the lodge. And I’ll tell them to take some sticks or tape to mark their way as they go. That may save you the trouble of having to go in and extract them yourself, Mr Humphreys.”
“A very good idea! Yes, do that. I’ll expect Mrs and Miss Cooper in the afternoon, and you at about half past ten in the morning.”
“It will be a pleasure, I’m sure, both for them and for me, Mr Humphreys. Good night!”

Humphreys dined at eight. Had it not been his first evening, and had Calton not been plainly inclined to occasional conversation, he would have finished the novel he had bought for the journey. As it was, he had to listen and respond to Calton’s impressions of the neighbourhood and the season. The season, it seemed, was seasonable. The neighbourhood had changed considerably, and not entirely for the worse, since Calton’s boyhood, which he had spent there. The village shop, in particular, had greatly improved since 1870. You could now get pretty much anything you might reasonably want. That was convenient, because if something was needed suddenly—and Calton had known such things happen before—he could go down there, provided the shop was still open, and order it to be sent up, unless he borrowed it from the rectory. In earlier days that would have been useless for anything except candles, soap, treacle or perhaps a penny picture book for a child. And nine times out of ten, what you needed would be something more like a bottle of whisky. At least—On the whole, Humphreys thought he would have a book ready in future.

The library was the obvious place to spend the hours after dinner. With a candle in his hand and a pipe in his mouth, he moved around the room for some time, looking over the book titles. He was naturally inclined to take an interest in an old library. Here he had every opportunity to make a systematic study of one, for Cooper had told him that no catalogue existed apart from the very superficial list made for settling the estate. Drawing up a detailed, annotated catalogue would be a delightful winter occupation. There were probably treasures to discover too, even manuscripts, if Cooper could be trusted.

As he made his rounds, he became aware—as most of us do in such places—of how utterly unreadable much of the collection was. “Editions of the classics and the Church Fathers, Picart’s Religious Ceremonies, and the Harleian Miscellany are all very well, I suppose. But who is ever going to read Tostatus Abulensis, or Pineda on Job, or a book like this?” He pulled out a small quarto volume, loose in its binding and missing the label that had once carried its title. Noticing that his coffee was waiting, he retired to a chair. Eventually he opened the book. It will be noticed that his condemnation had rested entirely on its outward appearance. For all he knew, it might have contained a collection of unique plays. But its exterior was undeniably blank and forbidding. In fact, it was a collection of sermons or meditations, and an incomplete one, with its first sheet missing. It seemed to date from the late seventeenth century. He turned the pages until a note in the margin caught his eye: “A Parable of This Unhappy Condition.” He thought he would see what talent the author possessed for imaginative writing. “I have heard or read,” the passage began, “of a man who, like Theseus in the Athenian tale, ventured into a labyrinth or maze. Whether this was a parable or a true account, I leave my reader to judge. This maze was not laid out like the work of our present-day topiary gardeners. It covered a wide area and was commonly believed to conceal unknown pitfalls and snares, and even sinister inhabitants that could be encountered only at the risk of one’s life. You may be sure that his friends did not fail to try to dissuade him. ‘Think of so-and-so,’ a brother said, ‘how he went the way you know, and was never seen again.’ ‘Or of that other man,’ the mother said, ‘who ventured only a little way in, and whose mind has been so troubled ever since that he cannot say what he saw and has not passed one good night.’ ‘And have you never heard,’ a neighbour cried, ‘of the faces seen looking over the high fences and between the bars of the gate?’ But none of it worked. The man was fixed on his purpose. It seems that the common fireside talk of that country held that, at the very heart and centre of the labyrinth, there was a jewel so valuable and rare that whoever found it would be rich for life. It would rightfully belong to anyone who persevered long enough to reach it. What then? Why say more? The adventurer passed through the gates. For a whole day his friends outside had no news of him, except perhaps the indistinct cries heard far away in the night. These made them turn in their restless beds and sweat with fear. They did not doubt that their son and brother had added one more name to the list of unfortunates who had suffered shipwreck on that voyage. Next day, they went weeping to the parish clerk to arrange for the bell to be tolled. Their way took them close to the gate of the labyrinth. They would have hurried past, in their horror of it, but suddenly they saw a man’s body lying in the road. Approaching it with feelings that can easily be imagined, they found the man they had given up for lost. He was not dead, though he lay unconscious in a state very like death. So those who had gone out as mourners came home rejoicing, and tried every means to revive their prodigal. When he came to himself and heard about their anxiety and their errand that morning, he said, ‘Yes, you may as well finish what you were doing. For although I have brought back the jewel’—he showed it to them, and it was indeed a rare piece—‘I have brought something back with it that will give me neither rest at night nor pleasure by day.’ They urgently pressed him to explain what he meant, and where this companion was who so turned his stomach. ‘Oh,’ he said, ‘it is here in my breast. I cannot escape it, whatever I do.’ It needed no wizard to help them guess that the memory of what he had seen was troubling him so strangely. For a long time, however, they could get little more out of him, and that only in broken fragments. At last they managed to piece together something like the following account. At first, while the sun was bright, he went cheerfully along, reached the heart of the labyrinth without difficulty, took the jewel and set out on his return in high spirits. But as night fell, when all the beasts of the forest move about, he began to notice some creature keeping pace with him. He thought it was peering at him from the next path. Whenever he stopped, this companion stopped too, which disturbed him considerably. Indeed, as the darkness grew, it seemed that there was more than one, perhaps even a whole band of followers. At least, that was what he judged from the rustling and cracking they made among the thickets. Now and then he also heard whispering, as though they were holding a conference. But no one could persuade him to say what he thought about who they were or what shape they had. When his listeners asked about the cries they had heard during the night, as mentioned above, he told them this. At about midnight, as far as he could judge, he heard his name called from a great distance. He would have sworn it was his brother calling. So he stood still and shouted at the top of his voice. He supposed that the echo, or the noise of his shouting, briefly concealed any quieter sounds. For when it became still again, he heard the soft tramp of running feet very close behind him. This frightened him so much that he began to run, and continued until dawn. Sometimes, when he ran out of breath, he threw himself flat on his face, hoping his pursuers would run past in the darkness. But at these times they always stopped, and he could hear them panting and sniffing like a hound that had lost the scent. This filled his mind with such extreme horror that he was forced to run again, turning and doubling back in the hope of throwing them off the scent. As though the effort itself were not terrible enough, he lived in constant fear of falling into one of the pits or traps he had heard about. He had, indeed, seen several with his own eyes, some at the sides of the paths and others in the middle. In the end, he said, no mortal creature had ever spent a more dreadful night than he had endured in that labyrinth. Neither the jewel in his bag nor the richest ever brought from the Indies could adequately repay him for what he had suffered.

“I shall spare my reader any further account of this man’s troubles, for I am confident that their intelligence will grasp the parallel I wish to draw. Is this jewel not a fitting symbol of the satisfaction a man may bring back from pursuing this world’s pleasures? And does the labyrinth not serve as an image of the world itself, where such a treasure, if common opinion is to be believed, lies stored away?”

At about this point, Humphreys thought a game of patience would make a pleasant change, and that the author’s ‘lesson’ from his parable could be left alone. He put the book back where he had found it, wondering whether his uncle had ever come across that passage. If so, had it worked on his imagination strongly enough to make him dislike the idea of a maze and decide to close the one in the garden? Not long afterwards, he went to bed.

Next day brought a morning of hard work with Mr Cooper. However excessive his language, he knew the estate’s business inside out. Mr Cooper was very cheerful that morning. He had not forgotten the order to clear the maze; the work was going on at that very moment. His daughter was on the tentacles of expectation about it. He also hoped that Humphreys had slept the sleep of the just, and that they would be favoured with more of this agreeable weather. At lunch he talked at length about the dining-room pictures and pointed out the portrait of the man who had built the temple and the maze. Humphreys examined it with considerable interest. It was the work of an Italian, painted when old Mr Wilson had visited Rome as a young man. Indeed, the Colosseum appeared in the background. A pale, thin face and large eyes were its characteristic features. In his hand was a partly unrolled sheet of paper. On it could be seen the plan of a circular building, very probably the temple, and part of a labyrinth. Humphreys stood on a chair to examine it, but it had not been painted clearly enough to be worth copying. Still, it gave him the idea of making a plan of his own maze and hanging it in the hall for visitors to use.

That same afternoon confirmed his decision. When Mrs and Miss Cooper arrived, eager to be introduced to the maze, he found himself completely unable to lead them to the centre. The gardeners had removed the markers they had used, and even Clutterham, summoned to help, proved as helpless as everyone else. “The point is, you see, Mr Wilson—I should say Humphreys—these mazes are deliberately made to look so much alike, to mislead you. Still, if you follow me, I think I can put you right. I’ll just put my hat down here as a starting point.” He stumped off and, five minutes later, brought everyone safely back to the hat. “Now, that’s very peculiar,” he said with a sheepish laugh. “I was certain I’d left that hat just opposite a bramble bush. And you can see for yourself there isn’t a bramble bush anywhere along this path. If you’ll allow me, Mr Humphreys—that is the name, isn’t it, sir?—I’ll just call in one of the men to mark the place.”

After repeated shouts, William Crack arrived. He had some difficulty reaching them. First he was seen or heard in an inner path, then, almost at the same moment, in an outer one. Eventually he joined them. They first asked for his advice, without success, then stationed him beside the hat, which Clutterham still thought it necessary to leave on the ground. Despite this strategy, they spent most of three-quarters of an hour wandering to no purpose. Seeing how tired Mrs Cooper was becoming, Humphreys finally had to suggest retreating for tea, with many apologies to Miss Cooper. “At least you’ve won your bet with Miss Foster,” he said. “You have been inside the maze. And I promise that the first thing I do will be to make a proper plan, with the route marked out for you to follow.” “That’s what’s needed, sir,” Clutterham said. “Someone to draw a plan and keep it handy. It could be very awkward if someone got in there and a shower of rain came on, and they couldn’t find their way out. It might be hours before we could get them out, unless you’d let me make a shortcut to the middle. What I mean is, take down a couple of trees in each hedge in a straight line, so you could see clearly right through. Of course, that would stop it being a maze, but I don’t know whether you’d approve of that.”
“No, I won’t have that done yet. I’ll make a plan first and give you a copy. Later, if we find a need for it, I’ll consider what you suggest.”

Humphreys was annoyed and ashamed by the afternoon’s failure. He could not rest without making another attempt that evening to reach the centre of the maze. Finding it without a single wrong turn only increased his irritation. He considered beginning his plan at once, but the light was fading. By the time he had gathered the necessary materials, it would be too dark to work.

Next morning, he carried a drawing board, pencils, compasses, cartridge paper and other materials into the maze. Some had been borrowed from the Coopers, others found in the library cupboards. Again he reached the middle without hesitation and set everything out. But something delayed his start. All the brambles and weeds covering the column and globe had now been cleared away, and for the first time he could see them properly. The column was plain, like those that usually support sundials. The globe was another matter. I have said that it was finely engraved with figures and inscriptions, and that Humphreys had at first taken it for a celestial globe. He soon found, however, that it did not match his memory of such objects. One feature seemed familiar: a winged serpent, Draco, encircled it roughly where the equator would be on a globe of the earth. But much of the upper hemisphere was covered by the outspread wings of a large figure, whose head was hidden by a ring at the pole, or very top of the globe. Around where the head should have been, he could make out the words “prince of darkness”. In the lower hemisphere, an area was covered in crossed lines and marked “shadow of death”. Nearby lay a range of mountains, with flames rising from a valley among them. Its label was—will you be surprised to hear this?—“valley of the sons of Hinnom”. Above and below Draco were outlines of various figures resembling the usual pictures of constellations, but not identical to them. A naked man raising a club, for example, was labelled Cain, not Hercules. Another, buried up to his waist in the earth and stretching out despairing arms, was Chore, not Ophiuchus. A third, hanging by his hair from a snakelike tree, was Absolon. Near him stood a man in long robes and a tall cap, inside a circle, addressing two shaggy demons hovering outside it. He was labelled “Hostanes the magician”, a character unfamiliar to Humphreys. The whole design seemed to assemble the patriarchs of evil, perhaps under the influence of a study of Dante. Humphreys thought it an unusual display of his great-grandfather’s taste. Then he reflected that the old man had probably picked it up in Italy and never bothered to look closely at it. Certainly, if he had valued it highly, he would not have left it exposed to wind and weather. Humphreys tapped the metal. It seemed hollow and not very thick. Turning away, he set to work on his plan. After half an hour he found he could not get on without a thread to guide him. He fetched a roll of twine from Clutterham and laid it along the paths from the entrance to the centre, tying the end to the ring on top of the globe. This enabled him to make a rough plan before lunch. In the afternoon he drew it out more neatly. Towards teatime, Mr Cooper joined him and showed great interest in his progress. “Now this—” Mr Cooper said, putting a hand on the globe, then hastily pulling it away. “Whew! It holds the heat to a surprising degree, doesn’t it, Mr Humphreys? I suppose this metal—it’s copper, isn’t it?—would be an insulator or a conductor, or whatever they call it.”
“The sun has been fairly strong this afternoon,” Humphreys said, avoiding the scientific question. “But I hadn’t noticed that the globe had grown hot.” He added, “No, it doesn’t feel very hot to me.”

“Odd!” Mr Cooper said. “Now, I can hardly bear to keep my hand on it. Something to do with our different temperaments, I suppose. I dare say you’re a chilly person, Mr Humphreys. I’m not, and that’s where the distinction lies. All this summer, if you’ll believe me, I’ve slept practically in my natural status, and had my morning bath as cold as I could get it. Day out and day in—let me help you with that string.”
“It’s all right, thank you. But I should be much obliged if you’d gather up some of these pencils and things lying around. Now, I think we have everything. We might go back to the house.”
They left the maze, Humphreys winding up the guiding thread as they went.
Rain fell during the night.

Most unfortunately, it turned out that the plan was the one thing they had forgotten the previous evening, whether through Cooper’s fault or not. As might be expected, the rain had ruined it. There was nothing to do but begin again, though this time the job would not take long. The guiding thread was laid out once more, and Humphreys made a fresh start. He had not done much, however, before Calton interrupted him with a telegram. His former chief in London wanted to consult him. It would only be a short interview, but the summons was urgent. This was annoying, though it did not really disrupt everything. A train was due in half an hour. Unless things went very badly, he could be back perhaps by five o’clock, certainly by eight. He gave Calton the plan to take into the house, but it was not worth removing the guiding thread.

Everything went as he had hoped. He spent a rather exciting evening in the library, having found a cupboard containing some of the rarer books. When he went up to bed, he was pleased that the servant had remembered to leave his curtains undrawn and his windows open. He put down his light and went to the window overlooking the garden and park. The moonlight was brilliant. In a few weeks, the resounding winds of autumn would break up all this calm. But now the distant woods lay deeply still. Dew shone on the sloping lawns, and the colours of some flowers could almost be guessed. Moonlight just caught the temple’s cornice and the curve of its lead dome. Humphreys had to admit that, seen like this, these fanciful creations of a past age had real beauty. In short, the light, the scent of the woods and the absolute quiet brought such warm old associations into his mind that he dwelt on them for a long, long time. As he turned away from the window, he felt he had never seen anything more complete of its kind. Only one feature struck him as out of place: a small Irish yew, thin and black, standing like an outpost of the shrubbery through which one approached the maze. He thought it might as well be removed. The surprising thing was that anyone had imagined it would look well there.

Next morning, however, in the rush of answering letters and going through books with Mr Cooper, he forgot the Irish yew. One letter that arrived that day must be mentioned. It was from the Lady Wardrop whom Miss Cooper had spoken of, renewing the request she had made to Mr Wilson. First, she explained that she was about to publish a Book of Mazes and very much wanted to include a plan of the Wilsthorpe maze. It would also be a great kindness if Mr Humphreys would let her see it soon, if he could let her see it at all, because she would shortly be going abroad for the winter. Her house at Bentley was nearby, so Humphreys sent a note by hand suggesting that she visit the very next day or the day after. We may say at once that the messenger brought back a most grateful reply. The next day would suit her admirably.
The day’s only other event was the successful completion of the maze’s plan.

Again the night was clear, bright and calm, and Humphreys lingered almost as long at his window. Just as he was about to draw the curtains, he remembered the Irish yew. But either a shadow had misled him the night before, or the shrub was not really as intrusive as he had imagined. In any case, he saw no reason to interfere with it. What he would remove, however, was a clump of dark growth that had taken possession of a space against the house wall and threatened to obscure one of the lower windows. It did not look as though it could possibly be worth keeping. Little as he could see of it, he imagined it damp and unhealthy.

Next day, a Friday—he had arrived at Wilsthorpe on Monday—Lady Wardrop came over in her car soon after lunch. She was a stout, elderly woman with a great deal to say on every sort of subject. She was particularly eager to be agreeable to Humphreys, whose ready acceptance of her request had pleased her greatly. They explored the place thoroughly together. Lady Wardrop’s opinion of her host plainly rose sky-high when she discovered that he really knew something about gardening. She joined enthusiastically in his plans for improvements, while agreeing that it would be vandalism to disturb the distinctive layout of the grounds near the house. The temple particularly delighted her. “Do you know, Mr Humphreys,” she said, “I think your estate manager must be right about those stone blocks with letters on them. One of my mazes—I’m sorry to say the stupid people have destroyed it now; it was at a place in Hampshire—had its path marked that way. They used tiles there, but with letters just like yours. Read in the right order, the letters formed an inscription. I forget what it said, something about Theseus and Ariadne. I have a copy, as well as a plan of that maze. How can people do such things! I shall never forgive you if you damage yours. Do you know they’re becoming very uncommon? Almost every year I hear of another being dug up. Now, do let’s go straight to it. Or, if you’re too busy, I know the way there perfectly, and I’m not afraid of getting lost. I know too much about mazes for that. Though I do remember missing my lunch—not so very long ago, either—because I got entangled in the one at Busbury. Well, of course, if you can come with me, that will be all the nicer.”

After this confident introduction, justice might seem to demand that the Wilsthorpe maze should thoroughly confuse Lady Wardrop. Nothing of the kind happened. Yet it is doubtful whether she enjoyed this new specimen as much as she had expected. She was certainly interested—keenly interested. She pointed out a series of small hollows in the ground which, she thought, marked where the lettered blocks had stood. She told Humphreys which other mazes most closely resembled his in layout, and explained that a maze’s plan usually made it possible to date it to within twenty years. She already knew that this one must date from about 1780, and its features were exactly what she would have expected. The globe, moreover, absorbed her completely. She had never seen anything like it and studied it for a long time. “I should like a rubbing of that,” she said, “if it could possibly be made. Yes, I’m sure you would be most kind about it, Mr Humphreys. But I do trust you won’t attempt it for my sake. I shouldn’t like to take liberties here. I have a feeling they might be resented. Now, admit it,” she continued, turning to face him, “don’t you feel—haven’t you felt ever since we came in—that we’re being watched? And that if we overstepped the mark in any way, there would be a—well, a pounce? No? I do, and I can’t get outside the gate too soon.”

“After all,” she said when they were walking back to the house, “perhaps it was only the lack of air and the dull heat in that place that pressed on my brain. Still, I’ll take back one thing I said. Perhaps I will forgive you after all if, next spring, I find you’ve had that maze dug up.”
“Whether or not that happens, you shall have the plan, Lady Wardrop. I’ve made one, and I can trace a copy for you this very evening.”
“Admirable. A pencil tracing, with the scale marked, is all I need. I can easily have it made to match my other illustrations. Many, many thanks.”
“Very well, you shall have it tomorrow. I wish you could help me solve my puzzle with the blocks.”

“What, those stones in the summer house? That is a puzzle. They aren’t in any sort of order? Of course not. But the men who laid them must have had instructions. Perhaps you’ll find a paper about it among your uncle’s things. If not, you’ll have to call in an expert on ciphers.”
“Please advise me about something else,” Humphreys said. “That bush-like thing under the library window. You would have it removed, wouldn’t you?”
“Which? That? Oh, I think not,” Lady Wardrop said. “I can’t see it very well from here, but it isn’t unsightly.”

“Perhaps you’re right. Only, when I looked out from my window just above it last night, I thought it took up too much room. It certainly doesn’t seem to from here. Very well, I’ll leave it alone for a while.”

Tea came next, and soon afterwards Lady Wardrop drove off. Halfway down the drive, however, she stopped the car and beckoned to Humphreys, who was still standing on the front-door steps. He ran over to catch her parting words. “It just occurs to me that it might be worth looking at the undersides of those stones. They must have been numbered, mustn’t they? Goodbye again. Home, please.”

At least the evening’s main occupation was settled. Tracing Lady Wardrop’s plan and carefully checking it against the original would take a couple of hours or more. Soon after nine, therefore, Humphreys had his materials laid out in the library and began. It was a still, stuffy evening. The windows had to stay open, and he had more than one horrifying encounter with a bat. These unnerving episodes kept him watching the window out of the corner of his eye. Once or twice he wondered whether something larger than a bat had a mind to join him. How unpleasant it would be if someone had slipped silently over the windowsill and was crouching on the floor!

He had finished tracing the plan. Now he had to compare it with the original and make sure he had not wrongly closed any paths or left any open. With one finger on each sheet, he followed the route from the entrance. There were one or two small mistakes, but near the centre was a serious muddle, probably caused by the arrival of the Second or Third Bat. Before correcting the copy, he carefully followed the last turns of the path on the original. Those, at least, were right. They led without a hitch into the central space. Here was something he need not reproduce on his copy: an ugly black spot about the size of a shilling. Ink? No. It looked like a hole, but how could a hole be there? He stared at it with tired eyes. The tracing had been hard work, and he felt drowsy and weighed down… But surely this was a very strange hole. It seemed to pass not just through the paper, but through the table beneath it. Yes, and through the floor below, down and still down, into endless depths. Utterly bewildered, he craned over it. Perhaps, as a child, you stared at a square inch of bedspread until it became a landscape of wooded hills, with perhaps even churches and houses. You lost all sense of its actual size, and your own. In the same way, this hole seemed for a moment to be the only thing in Humphreys’s world. For some reason he hated it from the start. But he stared for several moments before feeling any anxiety. Then it came, stronger and stronger: the horror that something might emerge, and a truly agonising certainty that a terror was on its way, from whose sight he would be unable to escape. Oh yes, far, far down, something was moving. And the movement was upwards, towards the surface. It came nearer and nearer, blackish-grey, with more than one dark hole. It took the shape of a face—a human face—a burnt human face. And with the loathsome writhing of a wasp creeping out of a rotten apple, something in the appearance of a body clambered out. It waved black arms, ready to clasp the head bending above them. In a convulsion of despair, Humphreys threw himself backwards, struck his head against a hanging lamp, and fell.

There was concussion, shock to his system, and a long period in bed. The doctor was badly puzzled, not by the symptoms, but by a request Humphreys made as soon as he could speak. “I wish you would open the ball in the maze.” “I should hardly have thought there was room,” was the best answer the doctor could find. “But that’s more in your line than mine. My dancing days are over.” Humphreys muttered, turned over and went to sleep. The doctor informed the nurses that their patient was not out of the woods yet. When he could express himself better, Humphreys explained what he meant and was promised that it would be done at once. He was so anxious to hear the result that next morning the doctor, who seemed a little thoughtful, realised that withholding his report would do more harm than good. “Well,” he said, “I’m afraid the ball is finished. The metal must have worn thin, I suppose. At any rate, it fell to pieces at the first blow of the chisel.” “Well? Do go on!” Humphreys said impatiently. “Oh! Of course, you want to know what we found inside. Well, it was half full of something like ashes.” “Ashes? What did you make of them?” “I haven’t examined them thoroughly yet. There’s hardly been time. But Cooper has decided—I dare say because of something I said—that it’s a case of cremation… Now, don’t excite yourself, my good sir. Yes, I must admit I think he’s probably right.”

The maze is gone, and Lady Wardrop has forgiven Humphreys. In fact, I believe he married her niece. She was also right to suspect that the stones in the temple had been numbered. A number had been painted underneath each one. A few had rubbed off, but enough remained for Humphreys to reconstruct the inscription. It read:
ENTERING INTO THE DEPTHS OF DEATH

Grateful as Humphreys was to his uncle’s memory, he could not quite forgive him for burning the journals and letters of the James Wilson who had given Wilsthorpe its maze and temple. No tradition survived about the circumstances of that ancestor’s death and burial. His will was almost the only accessible record of him. It left an unusually generous legacy to a servant with an Italian name.

Mr Cooper’s view is that, humanly speaking, all these many solemn events have a meaning for us, if only our limited intelligence would allow us to disintegrate it. Mr Calton has been reminded of an aunt, now no longer with us, who, around 1866, was lost for more than an hour and a half in the maze at Covent Gardens—or perhaps it was Hampton Court.

One of the strangest things in this whole series of events is that the book containing the parable has completely disappeared. Humphreys has never been able to find it since he copied out the passage to send to Lady Wardrop.
